lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- If You Move on Price
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 7 -- If You Move on Price

listenings.text: The negotiation is decided before anybody speaks, and what decides it is a single piece of paper I write the night before. Three columns. What I must have, what I would like, and what I am willing to give away to get the first column. That third column is the one people never prepare, and it is the only one that moves a room. If you arrive with nothing to trade, every request you make sounds like a demand, and the other side has no way to say yes without losing. The second thing on that paper is my walk-away point, written down, with a number, because a walk-away point that lives only in your head is not a walk-away point. It is a mood. I have crossed my own line exactly twice in twenty years and I regretted it both times, and in both cases I knew I was doing it while I was doing it.

We walked away from a deal three years ago and it is still the best decision I have been part of. The terms were fine. The cap was reasonable, the timetable was tight but workable, and if the discussion had stayed on the commercial points I think we would have signed within a fortnight. What killed it was one clause and the way they defended it. Every time we pushed back on the indemnity they explained why we were misunderstanding it, and by the fourth call I stopped believing that the misunderstanding was ours. So my client asked me the question that ends most negotiations properly. He said, if they behave like this while they still want something from us, how will they behave in eighteen months when they do not. I did not have an answer. We were on a plane home the next morning and neither of us has ever mentioned it with regret.
